spots.name: Lalbagh Botanical Garden
spots.label: Lalbagh

text.geographic_location: Lalbagh Botanical Garden is a large public garden in Bangalore. The Glass House stands on a lawn inside the garden.
text.access_note: Lalbagh is a garden with a gate, so check the official site before you go, and check on the day whether phone photography is free.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so make your own way to Lalbagh Botanical Garden in Bangalore. Once inside the garden, head for the Glass House and its south lawn, which is where the classic head-on view is taken. Check the garden's official site for which gate to use. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description:
Lalbagh is a large botanical garden in Bangalore, and its Glass House is the structure most visitors want a picture of. Guides call it the garden's most photographed building, and it is easy to see why. The iron-and-glass facade and the dome sit behind an open lawn, so the whole building fits in one frame without you having to step back into the trees.

The best photo is the classic head-on view. From the south lawn, facing the facade, you can line up the dome in the middle of the frame and let the building look symmetrical. One guide recommends doing this in the morning, and that suits a phone well, because the glass is less likely to blow out to white in softer light. The inside of the Glass House is normally closed, so plan to shoot the outside unless a flower show is on.

If you have time, the garden has other good frames. Lalbagh Rock is a granite outcrop with a wide view over the treetops and the city, and a 16th-century watchtower stands there. The lake bridge gives tree reflections on still water, with a small island and tree-lined banks on both sides. Both make a nice second or third picture after the Glass House.

Take your time on the lawn. Walk a few steps left or right until the dome is centred, and keep an eye out for people crossing the grass, who can add scale or spoil the symmetry.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the dome on the centre line, so the two halves of the building mirror each other. Keep some lawn in the bottom of the frame to lead the eye in. For a different view, Lalbagh Rock gives a wide shot over the treetops and city with the old watchtower, and the lake bridge gives tree reflections on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before about 10 AM, when the light is best and the glass is less likely to be overexposed.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the lawn, which lets the whole facade and dome fit with a little grass in front. If the lawn is busy and you have to stand close, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to keep the dome in frame, and keep the phone level so the sides do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glass or the dome to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright glass keeps its detail and does not turn white.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Glass House (front lawn to the south, facing the facade). The full iron-and-glass facade and dome of the Glass House, framed across the open lawn. Inside the garden, stand on the south lawn in front of the Glass House, facing the facade. From here the full iron-and-glass front and the dome are framed across the open grass.

spots.name: Bangalore Palace
spots.label: Bangalore Palace

text.geographic_location: Bangalore Palace is in the north of Bangalore, about 5.3 km north of the city centre.
text.access_note: The palace complex is open to visitors, but entry and photography rules (especially indoors) can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop information is available for this spot. The palace is about 5.3 km north of the city centre. The palace itself lies to the north-east of that point, about 7 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description:
Bangalore Palace is a royal palace built for Chamarajendra Wadiyar X, the Maharaja of Mysore, and commissioned in 1873. Its design is based on Windsor Castle in England, in the Tudor Revival style, so it looks more like a small English castle than anything else in the city. That makes it easy to photograph. You get large fortified towers, turreted parapets and walls partly covered in climbing plants, all set behind open lawns. The palace has about 34 rooms and sits roughly 5.3 km north of the city centre.

For a first picture, start on Palace Road in front of the ornate main gate. From here you can photograph the gateway and the approach to the grounds, with the first glimpse of the palace facade beyond. The gate details are worth a close-up. Once you are inside the grounds, the full front view with the turrets framed against lawn and sky is the classic shot. If it is busy, the rear and side of the palace with the garden in the foreground is a quieter alternative.

The grounds are used for concerts, fairs and weddings, so the scene can change from day to day. Interior photography is restricted, so ask at the entrance before taking your phone inside. Some rooms may also be closed for renovation.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the gate in the foreground, with the palace sitting beyond it. Move closer to photograph the gate's detailing. For the full front view of the turrets against lawn and sky, or the quieter rear and side view with the garden in front, you will need to go into the grounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when the low light is soft and warm on the gate and facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and the first glimpse of the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole gateway and lawns in one frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the turrets and gate details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate or the palace walls to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail. Keep the phone level to stop the towers leaning.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Palace Road (in front of the palace's ornate main gate). The ornate gateway and the approach to the palace grounds, with the first glimpse of the facade beyond. From here you see the ornate gateway and the approach to the palace grounds, with the first glimpse of the facade beyond. The palace itself is to the north-east.

spots.name: M. Chinnaswamy Stadium
spots.label: Chinnaswamy Stadium

text.geographic_location: In the middle of Bangalore, beside Cubbon Park and Queens Road, a short distance from MG Road.
text.access_note: The best viewpoint is inside the stadium and needs a ticket for an event, so check the official site before you go for current rules and which stands are open.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Queens Road at the edge of Cubbon Park, near MG Road, by taxi or hired scooter. The stadium is next to Cubbon Park and Queens Road. On match days expect heavy crowds around the gates, so allow extra time and follow the signs for your stand. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description: M. Chinnaswamy Stadium is Bengaluru's best-known cricket ground, on the edge of Cubbon Park and close to MG Road. Work began in 1970, and the first Test was played here in November 1974. It holds about 40,000 people and is home to Karnataka's teams and to Royal Challengers Bangalore, whose red and yellow colours give the place a bold look. It was also the first cricket stadium in the world to use solar panels for much of its electricity. For a phone photographer the appeal is the sheer shape of the place: a big open bowl, a neat green field and the pitch at its centre. The best view recommended here is from the upper tier of the G stand, which looks across the whole ground. That makes it a good spot for wide, sweeping shots rather than close-ups. Seats in the stands need a ticket, so this is not a free roadside viewpoint. If you only want the outside, the front facade with its large lettering can be framed from Queens Road at gates 1 and 2. Crowds build up outside on big match days, so take the outside shot on a quieter day. Photography rules inside have varied over the years, and the stadium has had restrictions on large events since 2025. Check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the field filling the lower half and the opposite stands and sky above. Try panorama mode for the full curve of the bowl, moving slowly and steadily. For a second viewpoint, the N stand also gives a view of the whole ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a ticketed match or event day for the full atmosphere. If it is an evening event under floodlights, try night mode and hold the phone steady against the rail or your arm. For the outside facade, pick a quieter non-event day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole bowl, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the field. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the pitch, the scoreboard or players.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the field to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the stands. If the crowd is moving, take a Live Photo or a burst and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The best-view recommendation is the upper tier of the G stand, which gives a wide view of the whole field and pitch and suits panoramic shots of the ground. This needs a ticket for an event. If you are only outside, the front facade is shown from Queens Road at gates 1 and 2, with the big 'Chinnaswamy Stadium' lettering.
